subsubtopic: SIGNING OF INTERNATIONAL PROTOCOL ON MEASURES TO PRESERVE OZONE LAYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to offer my congratulations to those countries which have succeeded in the achievement of an international protocol concerning regulatory measures for the protection of the ozone layer.
Earlier this afternoon in Montreal, Canada, represented by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), plus more than 50 other nations, as well as the European Economic Community, concluded the Montreal protocol on substances which deplete the ozone layer.
This agreement will see a scheduled reduction over 10 years of 50 per cent of the 1986 production levels of CFCs, or chloroflurocarbons. This chemical is closely linked with the destruction of the ozone layer which protects the earth from harmful ultraviolet rays of the sun.
To succeed in reaching an agreement among so many countries with different economic and production needs and obligations is no mean feat. Canada has been acknowledged for the important role it played in this achievement. Although we are responsible for only 2 per cent to 3 per cent of world production of CFCs, we took other nations to task to respond to the problem of the destruction of the ozone layer. I congratulate the Minister of the Environment and the whole Canadian delegation for their strong leadership, not only in getting the show on the road but seeing it through to its successful culmination.

On behalf of the New Democratic Party and all our constituents, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank most sincerely all the teams which took part in the Canada Cup tournament-

-for providing hockey fans around the world with the best hockey championship in over a decade.
Hear, hear!

Team Canada kept everyone on tenterhooks every night but in the final seconds of the last game they won it, and they won it in style. Showing tremendous courage and skill and making believers out of hockey fans everywhere, they demonstrated that you do not have to be Canadian to play hockey but it sure helps. To the players on Team Canada, thank you. Inside and outside Canada, on and off the ice, you are number one. Felicitation!

subsubtopic: EARLY AND TEMPORARY RELEASE OF PRISON INMATES- TOUGHER APPROACH URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the National Parole Board study found that more than 100 killings over the past 12 years were committed by inmates released early from prison.
Recently a day pass was granted to a convicted killer serving time in the Edmonton maximum security facility so that he could spend his birthday enjoying the thrills of the West Edmonton Mall. Although he was escorted he managed to escape and remained at large for some two and a half months before being recaptured. He has now been charged with two more counts of murder which he allegedly committed during his time at large.
I do not envy the National Parole Board. Their work is the kind where a 100 per cent success rate is impossible, but I must ask how many more innocent victims must pay the price before we toughen our approach to early and temporary release?
I said it on June 30 following the capital punishment vote and I say it again today: let us turn our attention to reform of the penal system. A life sentence should mean exactly that. Let us make the law work to protect Canadians.

subtopic: REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
REMOVAL OF RESTRICTIONS ON NATURAL GAS EXPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great decision has been made for Canada. The National Energy Board announced on September 9 a new procedure for determining the surplus of natural gas in Canada available for export. This is history being made. This is freeing the natural gas industry from government regulation.
Under the old system producers could not sell to the U.S. market unless they had a 15-year supply of gas available for sale in Canada. The Board has announced it will scrap the surplus test and allow exports to be determined by supply and demand. Market forces will operate freely as long as they are serving Canadian needs adequately and fairly. The Board can intervene if it finds increased exports could cause market difficulty in meeting Canadians' gas requirements.
This decision is a win for everyone. It shows that the free enterprise system can and will work. Congratulations to the Board and to the Chairman of the National Energy Board, Mr. Roland Priddle.
September 16, 1987

This week the Public Service Commission informed Mr. Brewer that he can get leave to run provided that he agree, if not elected, to move to Halifax after the election, an intolerable condition upon which to be allowed to participate.
The Public Service Commission informed my staff today that if someone in Mr. Brewer's position living in Ottawa had sought a nomination in the Ottawa area they would have been allowed to run without being required to move. During the 1984 election campaign the Progressive Conservative Party made explicit promises to grant federal public servants the right to participate fully in the political process. I regret that those promises have not been fulfilled. It is time they were because it is not fair that men and women who work for the Government of Canada are discriminated against in the way that Mr. Brewer is being discriminated against in New Brunswick.

subsubtopic: SIGNING OF INTERNATIONAL PROTOCOL ON MEASURES TO PROTECT OZONE LAYER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the adoption of an international protocol on ozone in Montreal is a historic step for all humanity and indeed all creatures of our planet.
Canadians can be justly proud of the role of our experts and officials in the difficult negotiations to reach this end.

As an Arctic country, Canada has more reasons than any other country to want the production of substances which are destroying the ozone in the atmosphere to be reduced or all together stopped. Our farms, fisheries, health and cities along the shores are the most quickly affected by the erosion of the ozone layer.

While we can be pleased with the adoption of a protocol, we would be fools to be satisfied with it.
Already much damage has been done and the CFCs which cause ozone destruction have a life span of 100 years.
Further vigorous measures will be required for our survival. May Canada continue to play a leading role in taking these next vital steps.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SCIENCE WORLD IN VANCOUVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year when millions of people visited Expo 86 in Vancouver, they were delighted by a glittering golf ball. I am pleased to commend the federal Government for its decision to provide $5 million to transform that Expo Globe into a world-class science centre for British Columbia.
It is appropriate that the spherical structure which was a symbol for Expo 86 will now become home to Science World. Science World will be a showcase of British Columbia's and Canada's achievement in science and technology, and as a hands-on facility will offer a unique opportunity to learn about the world of science.
Science World will also provide significant economic benefits. As a major tourist attraction it will attract thousands of visitors to thrill and wonder in the marvellous setting of the Expo Globe.
I want to pay special tribute to the efforts of British Columbia's Arts, Sciences and Technology Society which has developed this project and will operate Science World when it opens in May, 1989.
Science World is an excellent example of how all levels of government and the private sector can work together to advance the interests of British Columbia and create delights for young and old alike.

speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that the Governor General in Council has appointed Robert Marleau, Esquire, as Clerk of the House of Commons in the place of Charles Beverley Koester, Esquire, C D., M.A., Ph.D., who has been appointed Clerk Emeritus.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF CLERK, DEPUTY CLERK, AND CLERK EMERITUS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!

Before joining the House in 1975, Dr. Koester, who holds a Ph.D. in history from the University of Alberta, had distinguished careers as a naval officer, scholar and teacher, and Clerk of the Legislative Assembly of Saskatchewan.
As Clerk Emeritus, Dr. Koester will constitute a unique resource of parliamentary insight and procedural knowledge. He will direct a critical research undertaking aimed ultimately at publishing an original comprehensive manual of procedure and practice in the House of Commons to serve as a definitive reference document for the Speaker and Members of the House of Commons. This project, known as the "Bourinot Project", was initially launched by Dr. Koester and involves an in-depth review and update of procedural reference material which has not been updated since 1916. The Project also involves the development of an extensive computerized database of procedural decisions of Speakers of the House of Commons going back to 1867.

Robert Marleau who succeeds Dr. Koester as Clerk of the House has, since joining the House staff in 1970, served in various positions in the procedural sector. subtopic: COASTING TRADE AND COMMERCIAL MARINE ACTIVITIES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on Bill C-52, which is a Bill with which most Members will not be familiar, with the possible exception of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who will be sitting on the legislative committee. I suspect, with his long experience in the House, he has run across this Bill because it goes back to the early times of Canadian history.
I know members of the committee will find it to be a fascinating Bill and I can assure members of the Opposition from both Parties-I believe they have already had delivered to their office complete briefing books with the same information I have as Parliamentary Secretary-that there is no intent at all that this be a partisan-type Bill. I think over-all it is in the best interests of the country. 1 can give Hon. Members the unreserved commitment that we are prepared to have any witnesses the Opposition Parties would like, as well as some of our own government Members, on parts of the Bill in order to have a clear explanation as to why any particular exception may be listed in the statute. I believe at committee stage we can have a full explanation of the Bill, all the same briefing information, and we will make whatever changes are appropriate at that time.
Provisions concerning the Canadian coasting trade are currently contained in Part XV of the Canada Shipping Act which goes back, I believe, to the turn of the century. Recently we adopted Bill C-39 which amended part of the Canada

September 16, 1987
Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act
Shipping Act to allow the Governor in Council to make regulations concerning the granting of waivers to foreign ships and the prescribing of terms, conditions and circumstances for the granting of those waivers. These amendments did not include, however, the substantive changes which are included in Bill C-52.
The purpose of this Bill is to reserve what is commonly known as the coasting trade and other commercial marine activities to Canadian ships in waters over which we have jurisdiction. Within the 12 mile territorial sea, all commercial marine activities will be reserved to Canadian ships in the offshore. Beyond the 12 mile territorial sea, all commercial marine activities related to the exploration and exploitation of non-living resources will be reserved to Canadian ships.
In my briefing, I wondered why it said: "non-living" resources. It means minerals because there is another law, the law of the sea, which applies, while the Fisheries Protection Act and other statutes apply to living resources. All of this can be clarified for any Member of the House who is interested when we get to committee stage.
I should point out that the Canadian Government recognizes the usefulness and, indeed, the necessity of allowing foreign flag ships to enter the Canadian coasting trade and the offshore to carry out work when no suitable Canadian flagship is available. Accordingly, a waiver system to ensure the availability of adequate shipping services under such conditions is an integral part of the new legislation. This waiver system reflects current practice under Part XV of the Canada Shipping Act and it is expected that no disruption to the industry will occur in the transition to the system proposed.
At the present time, Mr. Speaker, you will be delighted to know that approximately 99 per cent of Canadian coasting trade is carried in Canadian ships.
"Coasting Trade" is defined in the Canada Shipping Act as including the carriage by water of goods or passengers from one port or place in Canada to another port or place in Canada. This Bill will expand this definition to include all commercial marine activities in the territorial sea and to cover resource related activities beyond the territorial sea to the edge of the continental shelf, or 200 miles, whichever is greater. I gather that there was some uncertainty in the existing statute as to whether dredging and the laying of cables could be said to be moving from place to place within Canada. This Bill has a more clear definition bringing these matters within the scope of the law.
With respect to the waters beyond the 12-mile territorial sea, Hon. Members will know that international law allows nations to legislate only with respect to the exploration and exploitation of natural resources. We have addressed this issue in the following ways.
Bill C-52 will reserve in this area all commercial marine activities related to resource exploration or exploitation to Canadian ships, always keeping in mind that the waiver system which I described earlier in the case of there being no adequate or appropriate Canadian ship available, with the exception of hydrocarbon production platforms. Hon. Members will note that the exception is not for drilling rigs, drill ships or other vessels in the exploration phase, but only for production platforms used in the exploitation phase.
Being interested in this industry I wondered why we would have that exception. I think that other Members will also want to have a clear explanation at the committee stage in this respect. We will come prepared to give such an explanation. If it is not adequate, then we may well make changes, if that is appropriate.
Our extension of coasting trade provisions to the continental shelf is intended to make the flag regime generally compatible with the tariff regime, which has been in effect since June 30, 1983. There are three exceptions to this. They are, production platforms, large cruise ships, and seismic ships. In addition, the inclusion of activity on the continental shelf will ensure maximum employment of the Canadian supply boat fleet, which has grown in anticipation of the development of Canada's offshore oil and gas activities. For we laymen, that means more jobs for Canadians and Canadian seamen-good news for us all.
Within the 12-mile territorial sea all commercial marine activities are reserved to Canadian ships. This makes it clear that ships carrying goods or passengers from one port or place in Canada to the same port or place in Canada are part of the coasting trade.
As an example, a cruise ship with overnight accommodations for fewer than 100 passengers which leaves from Montreal and returns to Montreal will be subject to the provisions of this Bill. In the previous statute under Part XV that was not clear. The Bill specifically exempts large cruise ships, those with overnight accommodation for 100 passengers or more from its application. This exemption recognizes that international cruise ships must carry on their business in a world-wide context and not exclusively in a Canadian one.
On the matter of exemptions to the legislation, a specific exemption is made for fishing vessels covered by the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, and for ships engaged in ocean research activity commissioned by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Similarly, exceptions are made for ships owned by foreign Governments wishing to conduct marine scientific research in waters over which Canada has jurisdiction, if they have been authorized by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This will ensure that conflicts with other legislation are minimized.
I know that Members opposite, like myself, will be seeking a clear explanation as to how all of these statutes fit together so that we do have a clear understanding of how this Bill fits into the whole scheme of legislation dealing with the sea.
September 16, 1987

In both offshore and Canadian waters ships assisting ships in distress will not be subject to the provisions of this Bill. This, of course, is normal international maritime practice.
The Bill will also eliminate the historic anomaly in Canadian legislation of referring to "British" ships rather than "Canadian" ships. Currently, only three British ships remain in the coasting trade.
I wish to address briefly the tariff implications of this Bill. At present, all tariff matters are the responsibility of my colleague, the Hon. Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). It therefore follows that the new coasting trade Bill contains no direct tariff provisions of any kind. This Bill will make flag requirements for ships compatible with the Canadian customs regime. These two regimes while not identical are very closely aligned. In fact, this Bill will ease the situation for those wishing to operate ships in waters under Canadian jurisdiction by clarifying the flag requirements which must be observed. The tariff schedule requirements are already well known.
Department officials have consulted the provinces on this Bill and I am advised that they support its thrust.
To summarize, the proposed coasting trade and commercial marine activities Bill will extend the jurisdiction of the existing coasting trade laws to include all commercial marine activities within 12 miles, with the exceptions I have already noted, and all commercial marine activities related to resource exploration and exploitation out to 200 miles, again with the exceptions I have noted.
This Bill will protect operators of Canadian flagships wishing to work in Canadian waters and on the continental shelf. As a consequence, jobs for Canadian seamen will be protected. As markets improve more job opportunities will be created for seamen and those in related industries.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on second reading of Bill C-52, also known as the Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act. Technically speaking, this Bill will enable us to update the Canada Shipping Act, Part XV, concerning the coasting trade in Canada. As a result of the adoption of this Bill, old Part XV will be repealed and replaced by a new legislation dealing specifically with coasting trade.
The basic aim of this measure is to modernize and update a piece of legislation which has not been revised for 50-odd years. It is obvious that a law reflecting post-war realities no longer meets the needs of Canada's merchant marine. 1 am therefore very pleased to join this debate today, and I can say that in this respect we are going through what I would call a very acceptable and even worthwhile exercise.
I commend the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, (Mr. Thacker) for keeping in mind that, before proceeding with the consideration of this Bill, Opposition

Members would appreciate receiving the kind of background information which will certainly help us gain a better understanding of the legislation. Such consideration on the part of the Parliamentary Secretary cannot however make up for the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) who seems to make it a point to stay away from the House whenever we are considering a measure which concerns his department. Again I must deplore this fact, but since I have had opportunities to get to know the Parliamentary Secretary even better and to appreciate his availability and competence, I will not hold it against the Government and the ever absent Minister.
But things get somewhat sour when, over and above the mere technical provisions of this Bill, we get to the basics of this legislative endeavour which, all things considered, is aimed at promoting the use of Canadian ships for coasting trade. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this is getting interesting. It is interesting because we can now examine more closely the whole shipbuilding policy of the Conservative Government, and I shall come back to this later on.
If I may go back a bit and look at Bill C-52 now under consideration, we find that the whole substance of this Bill resides in Clauses 3 and 4. Clause 3, for instance, prohibits any foreign ship or non-duty paid ship, except under and in accordance with a licence, to engage in the coasting trade or, and I quote:
(a)	in Canadian waters, engage in any marine activity of a commercial nature; or
(b)	in waters above the continental shelf of Canada, engage in any marine activities of a commercial nature relating to the exploration, development, production or transportation of the mineral or non-living natural resources of the continental shelf.
In order to obtain a licence to operate in Canada, a foreign ship must meet certain requirements set out in Clause 4, the most important being that the Canadian Transport Commission must have determined that no Canadian ship or non-duty ship is suitable to provide the service or perform the activity described in the application. In other words, it is to give priority to Canadian ships in the coasting trade of Canada.
We of the Liberal Party welcome this initiative. Indeed, we accept that it is an appropriate objective for the Government of Canada. On this side of the House we welcome any initiative which will strengthen Canada's shipping and shipbuilding industry. To ensure that this objective could be met, we had hoped that the Bill would have gone further in protecting Canada's interest in this crucial economic sector. Had the Minister read the American Jones Act of 1920, perhaps he may have been tempted to strengthen the Canadian legislation. He may have wished to fashion it in order to be more in tune with what the Americans have done to protect their shipping and shipbuilding interests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate on Bill C-52 respecting the Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act.
Let me say at the outset that the concept of restricting coastal trading to Canadians is obviusly one we support. We have argued for years for the need in the marine sector and in other sectors to enhance the ability of Canadians to build, to operate, and to improve the country. The same applies to coastal shipping.
This applies not only to coastal shipping, but to shipping within Canada. Although we talk about the Great Lakes as the fourth sea coast in terms of maritime law, we cannot describe it as such. However, I understand that the Bill will clearly deal with that matter as well. Therefore all our coasts are involved.
I think it is important to put on record some of the components of the Bill so that we develop an understanding of the steps through which we go. Let me start with the definition of "Canadian ship''. In part Clause 2 reads:
-"Canadian ship" means a ship
(a)	registered in Canada in respect of which all duties and taxes under the Customs Tariff and the Excise Tax Act have been paid, or
(b)	built in Canada and exempted from registration pursuant to section 8 of the Canada Shipping Act-
That sounds great. What it really means, though, is that it does not have to be built in Canada. It does not have to be owned by Canadians. It does, however, have to be crewed by Canadian citizens and it must be registered.
Let us compare that with the American Jones Act of 1920. When we see a good thing, I wonder why we are sometimes so slow to pick up on it. The Jones Act was enacted 67 years ago. It requires that domestic trade between U.S. ports must be carried by U.S.-registered vessels. There is no difference between that legislation and our legislation in that respect. The American legislation goes on to say that the ships must be owned by Americans and built in U.S. shipyards. Our legislation is different in those respects. The American legislation says that the boats must be crewed by American citizens and there is no difference there with our legislation.
The American law gives the maximum protection to American workers and maritime industries including shipbuilding and ship-repair facilities. We in this Party believe that we should do whatever we can to reach that same ideal. We should give the workers the maximum protection and the maximum incentive.

September 16, 1987
Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act
We all know that the Canadian shipbuilding and ship repair industries are in a crisis. The Government of Canada is making a conscious effort to rationalize the shipyards because their capacity is in excess of the contracts that exist.
Legislation is a tool that may be used for economic purposes. My colleagues and I believe that we should use this particular Bill as a tool to improve the lot of those people who work in our maritime industries, particularly those whose jobs and whose very existences depend on the ability of the industry to create new vessels, whether they be lakers, salters, icebreakers, fishing vessels or tugs.
We as a country have a responsibility to do what we can to help maritime facilities in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario, British Columbia and even Manitoba which has a small shipbuilding sector. All these facilities would be enhanced by a piece of legislation that would maximize our ability to build Canadian ships, to crew Canadian ships, to own Canadian ships and not to bring vessels and crews from offshore. We should not allow vessels of other countries to trade between Canadian ports unless they get an exemption.
Let me deal with the regulations that would allow exemptions for foreign ships and for what are called non-duty-paid ships. First let us define a foreign ship. It means a ship other than a Canadian ship or a non-duty-paid ship. What is a nonduty-paid ship? It is a ship registered in Canada in respect of which all duties and taxes under the Customs Tariff and the Excise Tax Act have not been paid.
If the powers that be have been told that there is not a Canadian vessel available or in fact even in existence to carry a certain commodity from one Canadian port to another Canadian port, an exemption can be sought. That exemption allows those ships to trade within our waters for a set period of time after paying certain dues or tariffs, I would suspect. However, this means that in the short term, that income is not available to Canadian vessels and workers.
I understand that in certain cases, there may not be vessels capable of carrying some unique cargoes. Over the last number of years, I have been aware of one such vessel that has been plying the Great Lakes during the winter months. It comes from overseas and is specially equipped to deal with icebreaking. It carries a chemical of sorts. It has been allowed an exemption for at least two years and perhaps for longer. I am not aware, though, of any attempt on the part of any arm of the Government to see an opportunity for a shipyard. Obviously there is a market for the movement of this commodity. The Government should see if it can put something together, perhaps totally under the private sector or under a mix of public and private sectors, to build such a vessel in Canada so that it can be crewed and owned by Canadians.
The situation could go on and on. It is kind of like imposing quotas to protect an industry that is either fledgling or does not yet exist in Canada. I can think of at least one industry that did not exist in Canada a few years ago, in one of the sporting goods fields. However, we never took the second step
which is to build up that fledgling industry so that it could compete not just in Canada but in the world market-place.
Let me deal with some of the other exemptions. I wish to express some concern about them. I appreciate the comments made by the Parliamentary Secretary earlier today about looking at this Bill in detail when we get into a legislative committee, and I look forward to that.
Clause 3 contains a list of exemptions to this particular clause. The clause does not apply to any foreign ship or to a non-duty-paid ship that is used as a hydrocarbon production platform. For those who are unfamiliar with the nuances of the search for oil and gas in the coastal areas of Canada, a drilling rig goes in first and then once whatever energy substance being sought is struck, the drilling rig is replaced with a platform. This exemption provides permission to bring a platform to Canada from some other country. It does not force the companies to build platforms here in Canada and to create jobs here in Canada.
I understand that the kind of platform that is used in the Atlantic is made to a certain extent out of concrete and can in fact be constructed in Newfoundland. Perhaps that is the case. I hope that testimony before the legislative committee will offer us the evidence we need to tell the Government that this exemption is no longer appropriate and must be removed from the Bill so that we can create jobs in Atlantic Canada and particularly in Newfoundland.

Another area I want to deal with is one I am less sure of because I have not had the opportunity to compare this Bill with previous legislation. However, some of my colleagues have expressed concern to me, and I hope during their presentations today they will be in a position to more forcefully and more knowledgeably explain those concerns. That area is with respect to Clause 3(2) which says in part:
(3) Subsection (1) does not apply to any foreign ship or non-duty paid ship that is
(b) used as a fishing vessel, as defined by the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act, in any activity governed by that Act and that does not carry any goods or passengers other than incidental to any activity governed by that Act;
The fear we have is that that kind of exemption would allow the continued importation of fishing vessels in excess of 100 feet. I gather if they are less than 100 feet they have to be built in Canada. However, the paying of duty on vessels over 100 feet does not create jobs on the West Coast, the East Coast, in Quebec or Ontario. It is important that we look at this exemption to make sure we are not continuing a loophole which, quite frankly, I think the Government would not want to continue.
I am not talking about a vessel which might come in for a month to replace a Canadian vessel under repair. I do not think any of us would suggest that. However, when we talk about additional capacity for harvesting of our marine
September 16, 1987

resources on an ongoing basis, then clearly those vessels should be constructed here and the jobs created here.
The other exemptions I think make a lot of sense, although perhaps there might be some reason to use a particular exemption as a triggering mechanism. For example, exemption (c) deals with a ship, as it states:
engaged in cruising, where the ship has overnight accommodation for one
hundred passengers or more;
Again, it is a balancing act.
I will give you an example. The City of Thunder Bay has applied to host the Commonwealth Games. Part of its proposal is to use cruise ships to provide 5,000 beds in order to accommodate the influx of tourists to watch the games. Part of the package involves a possible cruise up to Thunder Bay, perhaps from St. John's, bringing people to the games. Those people would then leave Thunder Bay by air, rail or bus. We probably do not have available in Canada enough vessels so we would have to get an exemption. If, on the other hand, should it happen that we rekindle the days of the Noronic and other passenger vessels which plyed the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence, and it became apparent that this was going to be a permanent arrangement, then that is when we say we must have a Canadian built, Canadian manned, and Canadian registered vessel. Some lead time would have to be allowed for financing and construction and you would not want to interrupt the ongoing service, but once the ships were ready we could say thank you to the people who loaned us the vessel or vessels and get on with doing our own job. We think that kind of thing is worth looking at.
Exemption (d) and (e) states:
engaged in any ocean research activity commissioned by the Department of
Fisheries and Oceans;
(e) operated or sponsored by a foreign government that has sought and received the consent of the Secretary of State for External Affairs to conduct marine scientific research;
I assume that is the Jacques Cousteau clause. Exemption
(0:
engaged in salvage operations, except where such operations are performed
in Canadian waters.
I suspect that means within the 200-mile limit. We might want to look at those once we get this into committee. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that there may be a need to allow for some additional protection. We have an ever growing industry in Canada that deals with robotics, underwater research, underwater manipulation of equipment, mini-subs and what have you. Perhaps we have to look at that as well to see whether we should be using this legislation as a tool to enhance that fledgling industry.
I do not want to continue dealing with this Bill clause by clause. I have made my point. Hopefully I have been able to plant some seeds in the minds of officials who I know are watching this debate and who will be appearing before us in committee, as well as the Parliamentary Secretary and his
Coasting Trade and Commercial Marine Activities Act
Minister. I recognize that the Minister is not in Ottawa, but is out performing his duties. We will take those things into account.
Let us come up with an even better Bill. Let us improve this so that when we finish third reading we can say we have done our share to promote the shipbuilding and ship repairing industry in this country. We have done it for Canadians, with Canadians. That is the goal we have to aim for.
One or two of my colleagues will want to add their comments. I think the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) will give us the perspective of the Pacific Coast and the impact there. The Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) will of course want to deal with Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada. Perhaps we will even hear from the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
I do not want to prolong the debate because I think it makes sense to get this Bill into committee and give time for those concerned and who have not yet seen the legislation, which is unfortunate, to have a chance to indicate what improvements we can make. I look forward to the rest of the debate and the improvements that will ensue over the next little while.

subtopic: COASTING TRADE AND COMMERCIAL MARINE ACTIVITIES ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate in the debate on the coasting trade in Canada. I would like to make the linkage between this legislation and the necessity for strengthening shipbuilding in Canada, and comment on some of the things we can do to improve this Bill in order to strengthen that industry. However, before I commence my remarks, I would like to comment on the remarks of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet).
When that Member was part of the Cabinet in previous Liberal Governments, those Governments visited a disaster on the shipbuilding industry and coastal trade in Canada. I sat in my seat amazed at the speech he gave in this House criticizing the Government. That criticism was absolutely ridiculous. The people who heard it must have been amazed. I met with delegations from regions of the country where shipbuilding was absolutely flattened, which delegations the Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), his Cabinet colleagues, and many elected Liberal Members of Parliament refused to even see. They refused to consider in any way, shape, or form the appeals they made to have some attention paid to the industry in order to have it strengthened.
The record of that Government was extremely bad with regard to the shipbuilding industry. It ignored and treated with contempt delegations from the industry, the communities which depended upon shipbuilding, and the workers who were laid off from the shipyards. Quite frankly, the record of that Government was disgusting.
During the election campaign of 1984 there was a great deal of optimism which was underpinned by Conservative promises
